title: Pairwise is not enough
objectives: Find three events that are independent in pairs but not all together
State mutual independence as a product rule for every group
Explain why pairwise checks miss joint risk

screens.title: Pairwise is not enough
screens.prose: Three events can each look unrelated to every other, two at a time. Yet together they can be tightly linked. Two coins are enough to show it.

state.caption: Two fair coins: four equally likely outcomes

screens.prose: Toss two fair coins. Let $A$ be “the first coin is heads” and $C$ be “the two coins match”. Before any news, $P(C) = \tfrac{1}{2}$.
screens.question: You learn $A$ happened. What happens to the chance of $C$?

options.text: It rises: $C$ is built from the first coin
options.why: $C$ does involve the first coin. But given $A$, $C$ needs a second head, and that has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

options.text: It falls: $C$ now needs a second head as well
options.why: Given $A$, $C$ needs a second head, which has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Before the news, a match also had chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

hints.text: Which outcomes are left once you know $A$?
Given $A$, only the first two rows remain.
Of HH and HT, $C$ holds in HH only. One out of two.

feedback.correct: Given $A$, $C$ holds in one of two outcomes: still $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the rows where $A$ holds, then count the ones where $C$ holds.

explain.text: Given $A$, only HH and HT remain, and $C$ holds in one: $P(C \mid A) = \tfrac{1}{2} = P(C)$. So $A$ and $C$ are independent, even though $C$ is built from the first coin.

screens.prose: Now look at $B$ and $C$. Tap a row to select an outcome; tap it again to clear it.
screens.question: Select every outcome in which both $B$ and $C$ happen.

hints.text: Read across each row: is the second coin heads, and do the coins match?
Only one row says Yes in both columns.

feedback.correct: Only HH has a second head and a match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Select the rows with Yes under both $B$ and $C$.

byKey.either: You selected outcomes where $B$ or $C$ happens. The question asks for both at once.
byKey.r3: TT is a match, but its second coin is tails.
byKey.r2: TH has a second head, but the coins differ.

explain.text: Only HH has both, so $P(B \cap C) = \tfrac{1}{4}$. That equals $P(B)\,P(C) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2}$. So $B$ and $C$ pass the product test too.

screens.prose: Events that pass the product test two at a time are **pairwise independent**. Check all three pairs. Each event has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
screens.question: Fill in $P(\text{both})$ and the product for each pair.

hints.text: Count the rows with Yes in both columns, out of four.
$A$ and $B$ both hold only in HH.
Every pair holds together in exactly one row, so $P(\text{both}) = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Every product is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each pair holds together in one of the four rows.

byKey.r0c1: $A$ and $B$ both hold only in HH: one row of four.
byKey.r1c1: $A$ and $C$ both hold only in HH: HT has $A$ but no match.
byKey.r2c1: $B$ and $C$ both hold only in HH: TT matches but has a tail second.

explain.text: Every pair holds together in exactly one outcome, HH, and every product is $\tfrac{1}{4}$. So $A$, $B$ and $C$ are pairwise independent. Learning any one of them says nothing about any other.

screens.prose: Pairwise independence passed. Now look at all three events at once.
screens.question: What is $P(A \cap B \cap C)$?

hints.text: Which rows say Yes three times?
Look at HH.
Only HH has all three: one row out of four.

feedback.correct: All three hold in HH only: $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the rows where all three columns say Yes.

byKey.product: You multiplied three halves. That is what full independence would give. Count the rows instead.
byKey.zero: HH has a first head, a second head and a match. All three happen there.

explain.text: All three happen only in HH: $\tfrac{1}{4}$. Independence of all three would need $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{8}$. So the three events are not independent together.

screens.prose: Each event alone tells you nothing about any other. Now you learn two of them.
screens.question: Given that $A$ and $B$ both happened, what is the chance of $C$?

options.why: You used the pairwise result. Each of $A$ and $B$ alone says nothing about $C$, but together they fix both coins.
That is $P(A \cap B \cap C)$ over all outcomes. Given $A$ and $B$, only HH is left.
Two heads do match. $C$ is certain, not impossible.

hints.text: Which outcome has both a first and a second head?
Only HH.
In HH the coins match, so $C$ holds.

feedback.correct: Two heads always match: $C$ is certain.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the outcomes where $A$ and $B$ both hold.

explain.text: Given $A$ and $B$, the outcome is HH, and the coins match. Any one event tells you nothing about another. Any two settle the third completely.

screens.prose: A risk model has three events, each with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. It checked every pair and found each pair independent. It now reports $P(\text{all three}) = \tfrac{1}{8}$.
screens.question: What do the pair checks alone tell you about $P(\text{all three})$?

options.why: You took pairwise checks as enough. Our coins pass every pair check, yet all three happen with chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

options.text: Only a range: anything from 0 to $\tfrac{1}{4}$ fits

options.why: That was our coins. If $C$ were “the coins differ”, every pair still passes, and all three never happen.

hints.text: The diagram shows our coin events. Do they pass every pair check?
All three meet in the centre.
Our coins pass every pair check with $P(\text{all three}) = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Swap $C$ for “coins differ” and it becomes 0.

feedback.correct: Pairs do not pin down the triple.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Our coins pass every pair check. What was their triple chance?

byKey.eighth: You took pairwise checks as enough. Our coins pass every pair check, yet all three happen with chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

explain.text: The centre holds $\tfrac{1}{4}$, not $\tfrac{1}{8}$, and every pair still passes. With “coins differ” as $C$ the centre would be empty. Three events need their own check.

screens.prose: Events are **mutually independent** when the product rule holds for every group of two or more. For three events that is four equations: $$P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B), \quad P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C),$$ $$P(B \cap C) = P(B)P(C), \quad P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A)P(B)P(C).$$
screens.question: How many equations does mutual independence need for four events?

options.why: You counted only the pairs. The coins showed that pairs are not enough.
You added the four-way equation to the six pairs. The four triples need checking too.
You counted the four single events. A group of one has no product to check.

hints.text: Count the groups of two, of three and of four.
Six pairs, four triples and one group of four: $6 + 4 + 1$.

feedback.correct: 6 pairs, 4 triples and 1 group of four.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every group of two or more events.

explain.text: Four events have 6 pairs, 4 triples and 1 group of all four: 11 equations. Every one can fail on its own, as the triple did for our coins. Only all of them together make the events mutually independent.

screens.prose: Test the definition at its edges. Think of our coins, and of an event with chance 0.
screens.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Mutually independent events are pairwise independent
Pairwise independent events are mutually independent
options.why: Our coins are pairwise independent, but the triple fails: $\tfrac{1}{4} \neq \tfrac{1}{8}$.

options.text: If $P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A)P(B)P(C)$, every pair is independent
options.why: If $P(C) = 0$, both sides are 0 whatever $A$ and $B$ are. Take $A = B$ with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$: that pair fails.

options.text: An event with chance 0 is independent of every event

hints.text: Which equations does the definition of mutual independence list?
The pair equations are part of the list.
Mutual includes the pairs. The coins break “pairwise gives mutual”. An event with chance 0 makes the triple equation read $0 = 0$.

feedback.correct: Mutual gives pairwise, but pairwise does not give mutual; a chance-0 event is independent of everything.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each statement against the coins or a chance-0 event.

explain.text: Mutual independence lists the pair equations, so it includes pairwise independence. The coins show pairwise is not enough, and a chance-0 event makes the triple equation hold for free. That same event passes every product test: $0 = 0 \times P(B)$.

screens.prose: Three assets. $X$ and $Y$ each rise or fall 1% with equal chance, independently. $Z$ falls exactly when $X$ and $Y$ move the same way. Each pair has zero correlation, and each pair is in fact independent.

state.caption: $Z$ falls exactly when $X$ and $Y$ move the same way

screens.question: What is the chance all three fall together?

hints.text: Which state has a fall in all three columns?
Look at state 4.
Only state 4 has all three down: chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

feedback.correct: All three fall in state 4, with chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the states where all three returns are negative.

byKey.indep: You multiplied three halves, as a model built from pairwise correlations would. Count the states: one in four.

explain.text: All three fall only in state 4: chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$. Treating zero pairwise correlation as full independence gives $\tfrac{1}{8}$, half the true crash risk. The danger lives in no single pair.

screens.prose: A risk system stores only the correlation matrix of $X$, $Y$ and $Z$: ones on the diagonal, zeros everywhere else. It sizes the book as if the three were unrelated.
screens.question: Why does this matrix miss the joint crash in state 4?

options.text: Each entry describes one pair, and the risk lives in all three together

options.why: The zeros are exactly right here. The problem is what a table of pairs can describe at all.

options.text: Moves of 1% are too small to matter
options.why: The size of the move is not the issue. The issue is that all three fall together twice as often as the matrix implies.
$X$ and $Y$ are independent by construction. Every pair here is independent.

hints.text: What does a single entry of the matrix measure?
Each entry compares two assets.
No entry looks at $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ at once, but the crash needs all three.

feedback.correct: A matrix of pairs cannot see a three-way pattern.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each entry of the matrix measures.

explain.text: Every entry is about one pair, and every pair here really is independent. The crash pattern needs all three at once, so no entry can show it. Joint tail risk needs joint data or a joint model, not just pairwise correlations.

ideas: Events can pass the product test in every pair and still fail it together: two coins with “first H”, “second H” and “match” do.
Mutual independence needs the product rule for every group of two or more events: four equations for three events.
Mutual independence implies pairwise independence, but pairwise does not imply mutual. Joint risk can hide from every pairwise check.

formula.name: Mutual independence of three events
formula.tex: P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A)\,P(B)\,P(C) \text{ and every pair independent}
formula.note: Neither part implies the other: check both. When several events are called independent with no other word, mutually independent is meant.

summary.trap: Checking only pairs. Pairwise independence does not fix the chance of all three together.

quiz.prose: Two fair coins. $A$ is “the first coin is heads” and $D$ is “the coins differ”.
quiz.question: Are $A$ and $D$ independent?

options.text: No: $D$ depends on the first coin
options.why: $D$ involves the first coin, but the test is about chances. Given $A$, $D$ needs a second tail: still $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
They can: HT has a first head and differing coins.

feedback.correct: Given a first head, the coins differ with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$, as before.

explain.text: Given $A$, the outcomes are HH and HT, and $D$ holds in HT. So $P(D \mid A) = \tfrac{1}{2} = P(D)$: independent.

quiz.prose: You want to show three events are mutually independent.
quiz.question: How many product equations must you check?

options.why: Those are the pairs. The triple needs its own check.
The triple alone is not enough: an event with chance 0 makes it hold for free.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every group of two or more.

explain.text: Three events form three pairs and one triple: four equations. Neither the pairs nor the triple alone is enough.

quiz.prose: Two fair coins. $A$ is “first heads”, $B$ is “second heads” and $D$ is “the coins differ”. These are pairwise independent.
quiz.question: What is $P(D \mid A \cap B)$?

options.why: You carried over the pairwise result. Given $A$ and $B$, the outcome is HH.
Two heads match, so they do not differ.
That is a chance over all four outcomes. Given $A$ and $B$, only HH is left.

feedback.correct: Given two heads, the coins cannot differ.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which outcome has two heads?

explain.text: Given $A$ and $B$, the outcome is HH, where the coins match. So $P(D \mid A \cap B) = 0$, although each pair is independent. Here all three never happen together.

options.text: No: only the triple equation is guaranteed
options.why: Mutual independence lists every group, and $A$ with $C$ is one of them.
The pair equation for $A$ and $C$ does not involve $B$. It is part of the definition.

feedback.correct: The pair equations are part of mutual independence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the equations mutual independence requires.

explain.text: Mutual independence requires the product rule for every group of two or more. The pair $A$, $C$ is one such group. So mutual implies pairwise.
